report:
## Report

The claim is well supported by strong evidence. Multiple large randomized trials and meta-analyses consistently show that bystander compression-only (hands-only) CPR improves survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) compared with no bystander CPR, and performs at least as well as conventional CPR with rescue breaths for adult, witnessed arrests.

Randomized evidence: The SOS-KANTO and Swedish/European trials (e.g., the NEJM 2010 trial comparing dispatcher-assisted compression-only vs. standard CPR) found 30-day survival of 8.7% with compression-only vs. 7.0% with standard CPR, showing compression-only CPR is non-inferior to conventional CPR (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0908991).

Meta-analytic evidence: A Lancet meta-analysis and companion PMC review found that dispatcher-assisted chest-compression-only bystander CPR was associated with improved survival compared with standard CPR involving ventilations, in adults (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(10)61454-7/fulltext; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2987687/).

Comparisons against no CPR: Population-based studies (e.g., Swedish registry data cited in secondary reporting) show that any bystander CPR—including hands-only—roughly doubles survival compared with no CPR at all, and rates of hands-only CPR use have risen sharply as survival improved in parallel (https://www.emergency-live.com/health-and-safety/survive-an-ohca-the-american-heart-association-revealed-that-hands-only-cpr-increases-survival-rate/).

Guideline endorsement: Based on this evidence base, the American Heart Association recommends untrained bystanders perform Hands-Only CPR for witnessed adult sudden collapse, reflecting consensus that this intervention meaningfully improves survival versus doing nothing (https://cpr.heart.org/en/resuscitation-science/cpr-and-ecc-guidelines/adult-basic-life-support).

**Conclusion:** The evidence—randomized trials, meta-analyses, and guideline bodies—robustly supports that hands-only bystander CPR increases survival after OHCA compared to no bystander CPR, particularly for witnessed adult arrests of presumed cardiac cause. Caveats apply for pediatric/asphyxial arrests, where rescue breaths remain important.
